## What the model is

This package contains a cohort Markov model of total hip replacement, a
simplified version of the model published by Fawsitt et al. (2019) that
compared prosthetic implant combinations using data from the UK National
Joint Registry (NJR) and the Swedish Hip Arthroplasty Register (SHAR).
It is used as the worked example in the tutorial on modularisation,
optimisation, documentation and testing of health economic models in R,
and this guide walks through running it from end to end.

The model compares four implant combinations for men aged 65 to 74
having a first total hip replacement:

| Implant        | Bearing surface         | Head size | Fixation       |
|----------------|-------------------------|-----------|----------------|
| Cemented       | Metal-on-polyethylene   | Small     | Cemented       |
| Uncemented     | Ceramic-on-polyethylene | Small     | Uncemented     |
| Hybrid         | Ceramic-on-polyethylene | Large     | Hybrid         |
| Reverse hybrid | Ceramic-on-polyethylene | Small     | Reverse hybrid |

Patients enter the model at age 65 in the post-THR state and are
followed for 30 one-year cycles. Each year they may stay where they are,
have a revision operation, or die.

## Health states

```{r model-diagram, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Model structure. Patients may need a first and then a second revision; the post-2nd-revision state also carries the cost of any further revisions. Death is possible from every living state."}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 6), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", asp = 1)
box_at <- function(x, y, label) {
  rect(x - 1.2, y - 0.5, x + 1.2, y + 0.5, col = "#EEF3F8", border = "#2C5F8A", lwd = 1.5)
  text(x, y, label, cex = 0.85)
}
box_at(1.5, 4.5, "Post THR")
box_at(5.0, 4.5, "Post 1st\nrevision")
box_at(8.5, 4.5, "Post 2nd\nrevision")
box_at(5.0, 1.0, "Dead")
arrows(2.75, 4.5, 3.75, 4.5, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
arrows(6.25, 4.5, 7.25, 4.5, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
arrows(1.5, 3.95, 3.7, 1.3, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
arrows(5.0, 3.95, 5.0, 1.55, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
arrows(8.5, 3.95, 6.3, 1.3, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
# Self loops: staying in a state, and further revisions from post 2nd revision
for (x in c(1.5, 5.0, 8.5)) {
  t <- seq(0.3, 2.85, length.out = 40)
  lines(x + 0.6 * cos(t), 5.0 + 0.45 * sin(t), lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(x + 0.6 * cos(0.35), 5.0 + 0.45 * sin(0.35), x + 0.6 * cos(0.3), 5.0 + 0.45 * sin(0.3), length = 0.07)
}
text(8.5, 5.75, "3rd+ revision (cost only)", cex = 0.7)
```

The four states are:

-   **Post THR**: living with the primary implant. Each year there is a
    small, implant-specific probability of a first revision.
-   **Post 1st revision**: living with the implant from the first
    revision. The probability of a second revision is the same for all
    implants.
-   **Post 2nd revision**: living after two or more revisions. Patients
    stay in this state, but each year they face a probability of a
    further revision that is charged as a cost without a change of
    state.
-   **Dead**: the absorbing state, reached from any living state with
    the age-specific probability from the UK life table.

## Setting up

The model functions are loaded with `devtools::load_all()`, which makes
every function in the `R/` folder available without installing the
package. In this repository the functions that take a `model_settings`
list are in `paper/R/`, alongside the original package functions, so
they are sourced from there.

```{r load-functions}
library(readxl)
for (function_file in list.files("paper/R", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) {
  source(function_file)
}
```

All structural settings of the model are collected in a single list that
is passed to every function. Changing the number of samples, the time
horizon or the discount rate means changing it here and nowhere else.

```{r model-settings}
model_settings <- list(
  n_samples      = 1000,
  n_cycles       = 30,        # 30 one-year cycles
  cycle_length   = 1,         # years
  initial_age    = 65,        # cohort starts at age 65
  discount_rate  = 0.035,     # 3.5% per year
  state_names    = c("post_thr", "post_1st_rev", "post_2nd_rev", "dead"),
  implant_names  = c("cemented", "uncemented", "hybrid", "reverse_hybrid"),
  data_directory = "data"     # data may be stored separately if sensitive
)
```

## Input data

All inputs are held in one workbook, `data/hips_input_data.xlsx`, with a
sheet for each type of parameter. Keeping them there, rather than in the
code, means a reviewer can check every number without running anything,
and the file can be stored separately if the data are sensitive. The
sheets are:

```{r input-sheets}
input_file <- file.path(model_settings$data_directory, "hips_input_data.xlsx")
excel_sheets(input_file)
```

First revision rates are the only inputs that differ between implants.
They are stored as log rates with a standard error, and sampled on the
log scale:

```{r input-revision}
knitr::kable(read_excel(input_file, sheet = "log_rates_1st_revision")[, c("Implant", "Mean", "SE")],
             digits = 3, caption = "Log rates of first revision by implant (NJR/SHAR)")
```

Second and higher revision rates are shared across implants, costs are
fixed, and state utilities are sampled from normal distributions:

```{r input-other}
knitr::kable(read_excel(input_file, sheet = "other_log_rates")[, c("Parameter", "Value")],
             digits = 3, caption = "Log rates of second and higher revision")
knitr::kable(read_excel(input_file, sheet = "costs")[, c("Resource", "Cost")],
             caption = "Costs (GBP, 2015-16 prices)")
knitr::kable(read_excel(input_file, sheet = "state_utilities")[, c("State", "Mean", "SE")],
             caption = "Health state utilities (UK PROMs)")
```

Mortality is taken from the `uk_lifetables` sheet, which the transition
matrix function reads itself because it is fixed and does not need to be
sampled.

## Running the model

The analysis is five function calls, each returning one object that the
next one needs. Setting the seed first makes the probabilistic samples
reproducible.

```{r run-model}
set.seed(123456)

input_parameters    <- generate_input_parameters(model_settings)
transition_matrices <- generate_transition_matrices(input_parameters, model_settings)
state_costs         <- generate_state_costs(input_parameters, model_settings)
state_qalys         <- generate_state_qalys(input_parameters, model_settings)

model_output <- generate_net_benefit(transition_matrices, state_costs,
                                     state_qalys, input_parameters,
                                     model_settings, lambda = 20000)
```

`input_parameters` has one row per probabilistic sample and one column
per parameter:

```{r input-parameters}
dim(input_parameters)
head(input_parameters[, 1:6], 3)
```

`model_output` is a list of four matrices, each with one row per implant
and one column per sample: `total_costs`, `total_qalys`, `net_benefit`
and `incremental_net_benefit` (relative to the first implant, cemented).

```{r output-structure}
str(model_output, max.level = 1)
```

## Results

Discounted lifetime costs and QALYs per patient, averaged over the
probabilistic samples:

```{r results-table}
lambda <- 20000
results <- data.frame(
  Implant = model_settings$implant_names,
  `Mean cost (GBP)` = rowMeans(model_output$total_costs),
  `Mean QALYs` = rowMeans(model_output$total_qalys),
  `Net benefit (GBP)` = rowMeans(model_output$net_benefit),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
results$`Incremental net benefit vs cemented (GBP)` <-
  results$`Net benefit (GBP)` - results$`Net benefit (GBP)`[1]
knitr::kable(results, digits = c(0, 0, 3, 0, 0),
             caption = "Mean discounted costs, QALYs and net benefit at GBP 20,000 per QALY")
```

The cost-effectiveness plane shows each sample's incremental cost and
QALYs for the three alternatives relative to the cemented implant:

```{r ce-plane, fig.cap = "Cost-effectiveness plane: incremental costs and QALYs versus the cemented implant, one point per probabilistic sample. The dashed line is the GBP 20,000 per QALY threshold."}
inc_costs <- sweep(model_output$total_costs, 2, model_output$total_costs[1, ])[-1, ]
inc_qalys <- sweep(model_output$total_qalys, 2, model_output$total_qalys[1, ])[-1, ]
colours <- c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = range(inc_qalys), ylim = range(inc_costs),
     xlab = "Incremental QALYs vs cemented", ylab = "Incremental cost vs cemented (GBP)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey70")
abline(a = 0, b = lambda, lty = 2)
for (i in 1:3) points(inc_qalys[i, ], inc_costs[i, ], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = adjustcolor(colours[i], 0.5))
legend("topleft", legend = rownames(inc_costs), col = colours, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve gives the probability that
each implant has the highest net benefit across a range of thresholds:

```{r ceac, fig.cap = "Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves."}
thresholds <- seq(0, 50000, by = 1000)
ceac <- sapply(thresholds, function(wtp) {
  nb <- model_output$total_qalys * wtp - model_output$total_costs
  best <- apply(nb, 2, which.max)
  tabulate(best, nbins = length(model_settings$implant_names)) / model_settings$n_samples
})
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
matplot(thresholds / 1000, t(ceac), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c("grey40", colours),
        xlab = "Willingness to pay (GBP thousand per QALY)", ylab = "Probability cost-effective",
        ylim = c(0, 1))
legend(0, 0.8, legend = model_settings$implant_names, col = c("grey40", colours), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The same results can be passed to the BCEA package for a fuller
analysis, including the expected value of perfect information:

```{r bcea, eval = FALSE}
library(BCEA)
hips_bcea <- bcea(e = t(model_output$total_qalys), c = t(model_output$total_costs),
                  ref = 1, interventions = model_settings$implant_names, Kmax = 50000)
summary(hips_bcea)
ceplane.plot(hips_bcea)
ceac.plot(hips_bcea)
evi.plot(hips_bcea)
```

## Reading the results

The cemented implant is the cheapest and the uncemented the most
effective, but the QALY differences between implants are small (a few
hundredths of a QALY over a lifetime) while the cost differences run to
over GBP 1,000, driven mainly by the price of the primary implant. At
GBP 20,000 per QALY the cemented implant has the highest expected net
benefit and is almost certain to be the cost-effective choice. The
acceptability curves show that this depends on the threshold: above
about GBP 28,000 per QALY the hybrid implant becomes the most likely to
be cost-effective, and above about GBP 42,000 the uncemented implant
does. This matches the finding of the full model by Fawsitt et al. that
cemented metal-on-polyethylene implants were the most cost-effective
option for this age group.

Because the probabilistic samples are drawn with a fixed seed,
re-running this vignette reproduces these numbers exactly. Changing
`n_samples` in `model_settings` will change them slightly; increasing it
narrows the Monte Carlo error of the means.

## Going further

-   `generate_net_benefit()` has a `method` argument. The default runs
    the original nested loops; `method = "vectorised"` gives the same
    results several times faster and is the version to use for large
    probabilistic or value-of-information analyses.
-   `optimisation/time_comparisons.R` benchmarks all the optimisation
    methods described in the tutorial.
-   `?generate_input_parameters` and the other help pages document each
    function's arguments and return values.

## References

Fawsitt CG, Thom HHZ, Hunt LP, et al. Choice of prosthetic implant
combinations in total hip replacement: cost-effectiveness analysis using
UK and Swedish hip joint registries data. *Value in Health*
2019;22(3):303-12.
